claims.text: NSAIDs ↓ bleeding by about 25–35% and relieve dysmenorrhea
claims.quote: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which reduce bleeding by approximately 25 to 35% and relieve dysmenorrhea by reducing prostaglandin levels (1)

claims.text: Tranexamic acid, given up to 5 days during menses, ↓ menstrual blood loss by about 50%
claims.quote: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that inhibits plasminogen activation that, when given for up to 5 days during menstruation, reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 50% (2, 3)

claims.text: COCs (cyclic or continuous) control bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction and ↓ volume in heavy bleeding (eg, fibroids, adenomyosis); progestin-only pills don't control heavy bleeding
claims.quote: COCs, used cyclically or continuously, can control abnormal uterine bleeding due to ovulatory dysfunction. Also, for women with heavy menstrual bleeding (eg, due to fibroids or adenomyosis), COCs decrease menstrual volume. Progestin-only oral contraceptives do not control heavy bleeding.

claims.text: Cyclic progestin: medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg/day or norethindrone acetate 2.5–5 mg/day orally for 21 days a month
claims.quote: Withdrawal bleeding may be more predictable with cyclic progestin therapy (medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg/day orally or norethindrone acetate 2.5 to 5 mg/day orally) given for 21 days a month than with a COC.

claims.text: Levonorgestrel IUD ↓ menstrual volume by about 70–95%, provides contraception and relieves dysmenorrhea
claims.quote: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD: It reduces menstrual volume by approximately 70 to 95% (4), provides contraception, and relieves dysmenorrhea;

claims.text: GnRH agonists or antagonists cause amenorrhea; used to shrink fibroids or stop heavy bleeding before surgery; hypoestrogenic effects limit use to 6 mo (add-back estrogen + progestin if longer)
claims.quote: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists or antagonists suppress ovarian hormone production and cause amenorrhea. They are used to shrink fibroids or stop heavy bleeding prior to surgical treatment. However, their hypoestrogenic adverse effects (eg, osteoporosis, menopausal symptoms) limit their use to 6 months. If long-term use is required, add-back low-dose estrogen and progestin therapy may be given.

claims.text: Danazol: taken continuously for about 3 mo; androgenic adverse effects, so usually used only when other therapy is contraindicated
claims.quote: Danazol reduces menstrual blood loss (by causing endometrial atrophy) but is not frequently used because it has many androgenic adverse effects, which may be lessened by using lower doses or a vaginal formulation. To be effective, danazol must be taken continuously, usually for about 3 months. It is usually used only when other forms of therapy are contraindicated.

claims.text: Iron (oral or IV) for iron deficiency anemia, if present
claims.quote: Iron (oral or intravenous) for iron deficiency anemia, if present

claims.text: Acute severe bleeding: high-dose monophasic COC (35 mcg ethinyl estradiol) TID x7 days;
claims.quote: High-dose estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives (OC): monophasic OCs that contain 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and progestin, 3 times daily for 7 days

claims.text: or medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg TID x7 days;
claims.quote: High-dose oral progestins: medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg, 3 times daily for 7 days

claims.text: or tranexamic acid 1.3 g PO or 10 mg/kg IV (max 600 mg) TID x5 days;
claims.quote: Antifibrinolytics: tranexamic acid 1.3 g orally or 10 mg/kg IV (maximum 600 mg), 3 times daily for 5 days

claims.text: or conjugated estrogens 25 mg IV q4–6 h for 4 doses
claims.quote: Intravenous estrogen: conjugated estrogens 25 mg IV, every 4 to 6 hours for a total of 4 doses

claims.text: High-dose estrogen, progestin or tranexamic acid ↑ thrombosis risk; after an acute regimen, a daily COC is usually continued until bleeding has been controlled for a few months
claims.quote: High-dose steroid estrogen, progestin, or tranexamic acid therapy is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis, so patient selection, education, and monitoring are important. After an acute management regimen is completed, patients are typically given a daily estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive, which may be continued until bleeding has been controlled for a few months.
